title: Leadership and Management Essentials
summary: Learn what managers do, leadership styles, motivation, decision-making and delegation, building teams and resolving conflict, and leading change ethically, with practical tools and worked examples.
audience: New and aspiring managers, team leaders, supervisors and student leaders

body.p: Management is getting things done through other people, using resources well. Leadership is influencing people towards a shared goal. Good managers need both: organising work and inspiring the people who do it.

list: Planning: setting goals and deciding how to reach them.
Organising: arranging people, tasks and resources, and deciding who reports to whom.
Leading: motivating, communicating and guiding people.
Controlling: measuring results against plans and correcting course.

body.p: Structure matters. Span of control is the number of people one manager supervises: 48 staff with 6 per supervisor need 48 / 6 = 8 supervisors. Wider spans mean fewer layers and faster decisions but less time per person; narrower spans suit complex or new work.

First-line managers (supervisors, team leaders) direct daily work; middle managers turn strategy into plans for departments; top managers set direction for the whole organisation. Moving from doing the work to leading others is one of the hardest career changes.

body.tip: As a new manager, your success is now measured by your team's results, not your own output.

body.p: There is no single best style; effective leaders adapt to the situation and the people.

list: Directive (authoritative): clear instructions; useful in emergencies or with new staff, but demotivating if overused.
Coaching: developing people through questions and feedback; best when people want to grow.
Participative (democratic): involving the team in decisions; builds commitment and uses their knowledge, but takes time.
Delegating: giving capable people ownership of outcomes.
Transformational: inspiring people with a vision and purpose beyond their immediate tasks.
Servant leadership: putting the team's needs and growth first so they can perform.

body.p: Situational leadership matches the style to each person's competence and commitment for a particular task: direct and support a willing beginner; coach someone who has lost confidence; delegate to an expert.

People follow leaders they trust. Trust comes from competence, honesty, consistency and showing that you care about people's interests. Admitting mistakes increases credibility rather than reducing it.

body.tip: Ask your team, "What should I start, stop and continue doing as your manager?" and act on at least one answer.

body.p: Motivation explains why people put effort into their work. Several classic theories still give practical guidance.

list: Maslow: people are driven by needs from basic (pay, safety) to higher (belonging, esteem, growth). Unmet basic needs crowd out everything else.

Herzberg: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, job security, fair policies) prevent dissatisfaction, but motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, interesting work, growth) create real motivation.
Expectancy theory: people try hard when they believe effort leads to performance, performance leads to rewards, and they value those rewards.
Self-determination theory: autonomy, mastery and purpose drive lasting motivation.
Pay fairly and on time; nothing else works if this fails.
Give specific recognition soon after good work.
Explain why tasks matter and how they help customers or communities.
Offer growth: new skills, responsibility and clear career paths.
Remove obstacles that make good work impossible.

body.tip: Ask each team member what motivates them; the answers differ more than most managers expect.

body.p: Managers make many decisions under time pressure and uncertainty. A structured approach improves quality: define the problem, gather facts, generate options, evaluate them against criteria, decide, then review the outcome.

To choose between two suppliers, weight the criteria: cost 50%, quality 30% and delivery 20%. Option A scores 8, 6 and 7, giving 0.5 x 8 + 0.3 x 6 + 0.2 x 7 = 7.2. Option B scores 6, 9 and 8, giving 3.0 + 2.7 + 1.6 = 7.3. B wins narrowly; when scores are this close, check the assumptions and risks before deciding.

list: Choose the right person and explain the outcome wanted, not just the steps.
Give authority and resources to match the responsibility.
Agree deadlines and check-in points; avoid hovering.
Accept that others may do it differently.
Recognise the result.

body.p: Delegation develops people and frees managers for work only they can do. If delegating saves a manager 12 hours a week for 50 working weeks, that is 600 hours a year.

body.tip: If you are the only person who can do a task, train someone now; it is a risk for the team as well as a load on you.

body.p: Teams often move through stages (Tuckman): forming (polite, unsure), storming (disagreements about roles and approach), norming (agreeing ways of working) and performing (working effectively together). Leaders guide teams through the storming stage rather than avoiding it.

list: A clear, shared goal.
Defined roles and responsibilities.
Psychological safety: people can raise problems and ideas without fear.
Regular, honest communication and feedback.
Mutual accountability for results.
Address issues early and privately.
Separate the person from the problem; describe behaviour and its effect.
Listen to each side fully and look for underlying interests.
Seek solutions both can accept, and agree follow-up.
Escalate harassment, discrimination or misconduct through formal procedures.

body.p: Some conflict about ideas is healthy and improves decisions; personal conflict harms teams and must be resolved.

body.tip: Hold short one-to-one meetings regularly; most conflicts can be solved early in a private conversation.

body.p: Organisations must change: new technology, competitors, laws and customer needs. Many change efforts fail because people's concerns are ignored.

steps: Explain why change is needed, with evidence and urgency.
Build a group of respected supporters.
Share a clear picture of the future.
Involve people, remove obstacles and provide training.
Celebrate early wins to build momentum.
Make the new ways part of normal practice.

body.p: Expect resistance: people worry about losing status, skills or jobs. Listen, be honest about what is known and not known, and support people through the transition.

list: Act with integrity, even when it costs short-term results.
Treat people fairly and without favouritism.
Refuse and report corruption.
Consider the effect of decisions on employees, customers, communities and the environment.
Set the example; teams copy what leaders do, not what they say.

body.tip: Communicate about change more often than feels necessary; silence fills up with rumours.

quiz.q: Which is one of the four functions of management?
48 staff with 6 per supervisor need how many supervisors?

options: Matching your style to each person's competence and commitment

quiz.q: According to Herzberg, which is a motivator rather than a hygiene factor?
Expectancy theory says people work hard when they believe:
options: Effort leads to performance and valued rewards

quiz.q: Option A scores 8, 6, 7 with weights 50%, 30%, 20%. Its weighted score is:
Option B scores 6, 9, 8 with the same weights. Its score is:

options: Giving authority and resources that match the responsibility

quiz.q: Saving 12 hours a week for 50 weeks frees how many hours a year?
In Tuckman's model, which stage involves disagreements about roles?

options: People can raise problems and ideas without fear

quiz.q: Why celebrate early wins during change?

options: Blaming the team for your mistakes
